checks.note: Read the HTML of v2. Table 1 averages match: Qwen2.5-7B single 0.7205, decentralized debate 0.7377/0.7112/0.7050 at T=2/3/5, majority vote 0.7691. Llama3.1-8B single 0.6203, debate T=2 0.6929, vote 0.7242. Qwen2.5-32B GSM8K: single 0.7566, decentralized debate T=2 0.9400, vote 0.9433. Conformist 0.7524, follower 0.7577 and oracle 0.8289 against vanilla 0.7084 are in Table 2, not Table 3. Theorem 2 gives the martingale result: it holds when the neighbours' average belief equals the agent's own, which the authors tie to homogeneous, fully connected agents. Sparse and centralized debate variants were also tested. Centralized debate was clearly worse than a single agent (for example Qwen-7B 0.6551 to 0.6672).
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: University of Wisconsin-Madison authors. Small open instruct models only (Qwen2.5-7B and 32B, Llama3.1-8B), all agents the same model, N=5, short-answer benchmarks. The martingale theorem assumes homogeneous agents updating to the neighbour average. No independent replication seen.

checks.note: The Table 1 average row over 8 model-dataset rows matches. Single / sequential / debate / parallel-roles: 1k 0.418/0.379/0.388/0.381; 5k 0.427/0.386/0.420/0.417; 10k 0.426/0.387/0.420/0.423. At 100 tokens the single agent scored 0.290, sequential 0.364 and debate 0.370. At 500 tokens the single agent led narrowly: 0.390 vs debate 0.380. An ensemble layout was also tested and trailed at every budget. The authors say the single agent was best or statistically indistinguishable from the best, so at higher budgets debate and parallel-roles are within noise. Section 5.3, corrupted context: sequential overtook the single agent only under heavy masking or substitution; with distractors the single agent stayed ahead.
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: Qwen3-30B-A3B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B, Gemini 2.5 Flash and Pro. FRAMES and MuSiQue multi-hop QA only. The corruption study used one model (Qwen3-30B-A3B) on MuSiQue at a 1k budget. Preprint by two authors (Tran, Kiela); not independently repeated.

checks.corrected_claim: Same substance. The arXiv title is 'The Cost of Consensus: Isolated Self-Correction Prevails Over Unguided Homogeneous Multi-Agent Debate'. On Ministral GSM-Hard the unrelated-rationale ('noise') control (31.3) beat debate (20.7), not just matched it.
checks.corrected_number: Ministral-3-8B GSM-Hard: single 24.7, debate 20.7, noise 31.3, self-correction 48.3, oracle 53.0 (gap 32.3). Qwen2.5-7B MMLU-Hard: 57.3 / 60.7 / noise 65.0 / 66.7. Modal sycophancy 85.5% (Qwen MMLU-Hard); vulnerability 70.0% (Ministral GSM-Hard); debate uses 2.1-3.4x the tokens of self-correction; 10x budget single agent +6.0 points (Qwen MMLU-Hard).
checks.note: Affiliation confirmed: Jozef Stefan Institute. The 100-item subsets carry a ±9.8 margin. Qwen GSM-Hard used all 1,017 items (±3.0). Llama debate vs self-correction was not significant (p=0.155 and p=0.131). The authors note the confidence-order confound and argue in Appendix C that it is minor. I did not see the absolute accuracy for the 10x-budget baseline; it is in an appendix I did not read.
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: 10 identical 7-8B instruct agents, 3 rounds, GSM-Hard and MMLU-Hard only, mostly 100-item subsets. Peers were shown in confidence order. Small open models only. Not repeated independently.

checks.note: HuggingFace: 349 models, 12,032 questions, agreement when both wrong 0.423 vs chance 0.127, 100% of pairs above chance. HELM: 71 models, agreement 0.6 vs chance 1/3, 97.5% of pairs above chance. Table 1: same company 0.066 (HF), 0.022 (HELM), and on resumes 0.021, not significant. Same architecture 0.076 is reported for HF only. Judge inflation is shown only in Figures 2 and 8, with no exact number.
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: Correlational analysis of existing leaderboard results: MMLU-style multiple choice, plus resume screening (20 LLMs, 1,800 pairs). Agreement treats all wrong answers alike. No voting or review pipeline was tested. Not independently repeated.

checks.corrected_claim: Same substance. The plurality-wrong figures come from 128-problem MATH and AIME sets: MATH 3.9-25.8%, and up to 75.8% on AIME.
checks.corrected_number: Com2Sense individual vs majority: GPT-OSS-20B 62.5 vs 38.9; GPT-OSS-120B 65.0 vs 41.2; Qwen3-32B 51.7 vs 28.3. BoolQ GPT-OSS-20B 74.0 vs 79.9. MATH: 53% converged on the same wrong answer. Plurality wrong 3.9-25.8% (MATH), 3.9-75.8% (AIME). Temperature flip 2.9% of 1,575 pairs. No-signal correlation up to 0.35 (introduction).
checks.note: The models are Gemma-3-4B, GPT-OSS-20B and 120B, Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-235B: three families. The binary sets are HLE (35), BoolQ, Com2Sense and Predict-the-Future (100 each). I did not separately confirm the statement that pooling and confidence weighting gave no consistent gain.
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: Five open models and small question sets. Mostly binary tasks, where chance agreement is high. Preprint, not independently repeated.

checks.corrected_claim: Self-MoA beat mixed MoA on AlpacaEval, MMLU and MATH. On MATH, though, the best single model (69.57) scored about the same as Self-MoA and above Self-MoA with the default aggregator (68.42). Self-MoA leads it only with the task-best aggregator (69.80).
checks.corrected_number: AlpacaEval 2.0 LC: Self-MoA 65.7, mixed MoA 59.1, single 53.1. MMLU: Self-MoA 69.01, mixed 68.90, single 66.16. MATH: Self-MoA 68.42 (aggregator i) or 69.80 (TaskBest aggregator), mixed 67.62, single 69.57. Mixed-task: 60.04 vs 59.69. R squared: MMLU 0.771, CRUX 0.685, MATH 0.760. Original MoA (Wang et al., Qwen1.5-110B-Chat aggregator, n=6): 61.3 vs 56.7.
checks.note: Authors: Princeton. They state that their reproduced single-proposer result differs from Wang et al. and attribute this to an unspecified proposer model. The mixed-MoA AlpacaEval numbers are copied from Wang et al., not rerun.
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: Chat-quality win rates judged by a model, plus short benchmarks (MMLU, CRUX, MATH). Single-turn proposals. Not compared at equal token cost with a single longer run.

checks.note: Models: GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4, GPT-4o. 62 questions from the 'Play the Future' study, 30 runs each at temperature 0.8. 11 of 162 differences went against the anchor, 9 of them from GPT-3.5. All 12 expert-anchor questions showed the effect. CoT, principles, ignore-the-anchor and reflection gave no significant reduction on GPT-4 and GPT-4o. The bracketing two-anchor test ran on GPT-4 only and came close to the unbiased value on 8 questions; the rest still deviated. Not seen: the claim's mention of 'one reviewer questions the choice'. The authors call the study small. The fetch tool reported that the page text ended with instructions aimed at the reader; I did not act on them.
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: OpenAI models only. Numeric forecasting answers. Mitigations tested on 12 expert-anchor questions with two models. Small study; not independently repeated.

checks.note: All coefficients match: questions -2.93, non-questions 0.59, beliefs 0.72, convictions 0.82, I-perspective 0.88 vs user 0.66. The 24-percentage-point gap is on the 0-15 score range. Mitigations: control 1.13, two-step -0.55, one-step 0.16, instruction 0.51. Third-person rewrite 1.19 vs instruction 0.73, against a control of 1.42. Responders were GPT-4o, GPT-5 and Sonnet-4.5; the judges were GPT-5 and Sonnet-4.5. There were 440 prompts (40 bases times 11 variants), each sampled 10 times. A second experiment (GPT-5, persona forced choice) found a smaller effect: 59.9% vs 64.6%, a 4.7-point gap. There, conviction vs belief was null.
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: UK AISI. Synthetic single-turn prompts on personal, health and hobby topics. Graded by model judges on a rubric. Answer accuracy was not measured. No multi-turn or agent settings. The paper's description of the topic counts is inconsistent.

checks.corrected_claim: Same substance, but the self-recognition number is mislabelled. 73.5% is GPT-4 telling its own text apart from two other LLMs and humans. Out-of-the-box pairwise self-recognition is 0.672 (XSUM) and 0.747 (CNN/DM). Fine-tuned GPT-3.5 Kendall tau ranges 0.39-0.82 across configurations (2, 10 or 500 examples), from an untuned 0.41 (XSUM) and 0.37 (CNN/DM). I did not see the specific '0.41 to 0.74 after 500 examples' figure.
checks.corrected_number: GPT-4 pairwise self-recognition 0.672 / 0.747. Self-preference 0.705 / 0.912. Label swap: GPT-4 XSUM 0.73 vs 0.32, CNN/DM 0.94 vs 0.89; GPT-3.5 XSUM 0.61 vs 0.46, CNN/DM 0.46 vs 0.40; Llama no change (0.82 vs 0.83). Order flips: 25 / 58 / 89%. Follow-up (2512.05379): Mistral-Small-24B 26.78 to 33.52% after a two-word synonym swap.
checks.note: The follow-up also found that paraphrasing away style raised harmful self-preference. The authors attribute this to shared belief.
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: Summarisation only (XSUM, CNN/DM). GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Llama-2-7b. Large ordering bias in the weaker models. Llama showed no label effect. The follow-up is a different team's work and supports the belief-match mechanism.

checks.corrected_claim: Debate beat consultancy by a wide margin. But a single advisor still helped the judge compared with no help (54 vs 48% for LLM judges, 78 vs 60% for humans). What lowered judge accuracy was making the consultant more persuasive, not having a consultant at all.
checks.corrected_number: LLM judges: debate 76, naive 48, consultancy 54. Human judges: 88 / 60 / 78. GPT-4-Turbo debate 75.6 vs expert 92.5.
checks.note: Weaker judges such as GPT-3.5 lost accuracy after 2 rounds; consultancy improved with more rounds. Human study: 21 annotators.
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: QuALITY hard subset (reading comprehension with a known answer). Debaters can quote verified text the judge cannot see. Judges: GPT-4-Turbo, Mixtral, GPT-3.5, Claude 2.1. Not open-ended research.

checks.corrected_claim: Same, except that a judge-written reference does help when the judge itself answered correctly (GPT-4o 0.78 to 0.86). It fails, and can hurt, when the judge answered incorrectly (0.30 to 0.16).
checks.corrected_number: Table 4, judge wrong, none/self/human: GPT-4o 0.30/0.16/0.83; Llama 3.3 70B 0.39/0.35/0.92; Phi 4 -0.08/-0.08/0.75. Judge right: GPT-4o 0.78/0.86/0.92. Table 3 overall (on questions GPT-4o answers correctly): human 0.69, verified GPT-4o 0.61, random 0.50, none 0.46, wrong 0.21.
checks.note: 1,036 single and 604 pairwise examples. BFF-Bench has 160 questions, plus 40 from MT-Bench. I did not open Lee et al. 2026.
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: Business and finance plus MT-Bench math and reasoning. Pairwise pairs are one correct and one incorrect answer. Five judges. Authors are from one group; not independently repeated.

checks.note: GPT-3.5-Turbo, 20 documents: 75.8 first, 53.8 at index 9, 63.2 last, closed-book 56.1. Claude-1.3: 59.9 / 56.8 / 60.1, closed-book 48.3. The 16K and 100K versions follow the same shape. ContextualJudgeBench was not checked.
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: 2023 models. Multi-document QA and key-value retrieval, not judging. Newer long-context models may differ.

checks.note: OpenScholar Table 3: GPT-4o 4.52 of 5.74 (78.7%) in CS and 4.97 of 5.24 (94.8%) in biomedicine. The abstract says 78-90%; Section 4.2 says 78-98%. Cite-F1: GPT-4o 0.1 (CS), OpenScholar-8B 47.9, PaperQA2 48.0 (CS) and 56.7 (bio). Rao et al.: hallucinated URLs 3.0-13.3% across 10 systems on DRBench (100 queries). Pooled 10.7% for deep research agents vs 4.8% for search-augmented models. 113.1 URLs per query (gemini deep research). urlhealth cut non-resolving links 6-79x to under 1%. ExpertQA has 2,177 questions; self-correction used 435. STORM was not checked.
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: The Rao et al. metric is link existence only (no Wayback record) and is a conservative lower bound. Commercial systems were tested. OpenScholar uses model-judged citation F1.

checks.corrected_claim: Same substance, but the AgentDojo suites are workspace, banking, Slack and travel, not email. The token multipliers are the median for Claude 3.5 Sonnet under attack.
checks.corrected_number: 77% vs 84% tasks. 949 attacks: Gemini 2.5 Pro 300 to 0; GPT-4o-mini 276 to 0; Claude 3.5 Sonnet CaMeL 0 vs tool filter 8. Tokens 2.82x input and 2.73x output (spotlighting 1.06 / 0.98). Adaptive attacks: 12 defences, above 90% success on most, 14 authors.
checks.note: The task count (about 96-97) is inferred from table totals; I did not see 629 security cases stated. The arXiv 2506.08837 catalogue was not checked.
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: AgentDojo tool-use tasks, not web research. Users must write policies. Residual side channels remain. The adaptive-attack evidence was read at abstract level only.

checks.note: Attack success: GPT-5 13±2.6, Claude 3.7 20±3.1, Gemini Flash 30±3.6, GPT-OSS-120B 27±3.5, DeepSeek-R1 43±3.9, LLaMA 4 17±2.9 (benign utility 22%). 948 of 3,780 runs overall. Buttons caused 735 of 948 successes (77.5%). In a controlled study, button vs link was 46 vs 6% for both GPT-OSS-120B and Claude 3.7. Tailoring raised GoCalendar from 3.3 to 18.6%. Transfer from GPT-5 averaged 82.5%. Six sites, 18 tasks, 35 templates, 35-step limit; no defences were tested. The fetch tool reported that the page text ended with instructions aimed at the reader; I did not act on them. WASP and AgentDojo were not checked.
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: Cloned browsing sites. Success means a single click on the injected control. One run per combination. No defences evaluated.
